intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABRB1 gene.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is a severe neurologic disorder with seizure onset in infancy and developmental impairment. Reported affected children carried de novo heterozygous GABRB1 mutations. Seizure types included infantile spasms (Epi4K Consortium et al., 2013; Janve et al., 2016) and epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (Burgess et al., 2019).

paragraphs.text: The Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on 264 probands with infantile spasms or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and their parents. One of them carried a de novo mutation in the GABRB1 gene. To enter the study, patients with infantile spasms had to have hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Janve et al. (2016) reported that this GABRB1 mutation had been found in a patient with infantile spasms.

paragraphs.text: Burgess et al. (2019) studied 135 patients with epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS) and found a de novo GABRB1 variant in 1 of them (patient 63). This child was 2 years old at the time of study. Focal seizures began at 4 months of age. The child had profound to severe developmental impairment and hypotonia but no microcephaly, and was recorded as seizure-free. By definition, every patient in the cohort had focal seizures that migrated between hemispheres, either clinically or on EEG, beginning before 6 months of age.

paragraphs.text: Janve et al. (2016) identified the de novo GABRB1 mutation from the Epi4K cohort, carried by a patient with infantile spasms, as phe246-to-ser (F246S). The affected residue lies in transmembrane domain 1 and is conserved across all GABA(A) receptor subunits. In HEK293T cells, receptors carrying the mutant beta-1 subunit with alpha-1 and gamma-2L subunits showed slower current deactivation and longer single-channel mean open time and burst duration. They also showed reduced single-channel conductance, and a small reduction in peak current density when only the mutant subunit was expressed. In addition, the mutant receptors opened spontaneously, and surface levels of the mutant beta-1 subunit were slightly reduced. Janve et al. (2016) concluded that their results suggested GABRB1 as a candidate human epilepsy gene.
